opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a few things, and honestly most of them are less about resources than people assume.

The first is the questions you're willing to ask. A frontier lab is working on problems where nobody knows yet whether the answer is even possible. In robotics that often means asking things like: can a robot generalize to a kitchen it has never seen? Can it learn a new skill from a handful of demonstrations instead of thousands? If your research agenda is mostly incremental, a few points better on a benchmark everyone already uses, you're doing good science, but you're not really at the frontier. The frontier is where the benchmarks don't exist yet because nobody has figured out how to measure the thing.

The second is closing the loop with the real world. Robotics is different from pure machine learning because reality is the final judge. You can have a beautiful result in simulation, and then you put it on hardware and it falls apart because of friction or latency or a cable snagging. The labs I think of as frontier labs have a very tight cycle between ideas, data, training, and physical deployment. They run real robots every day. They treat hardware failures as information instead of as an annoyance. That loop speed matters enormously.

Third, and related, is data. For a long time robotics was bottlenecked on algorithms, and now I think it's much more bottlenecked on data and on infrastructure for collecting it. A frontier lab is thinking seriously about how you scale data collection, whether through teleoperation, low-cost hardware, human videos, or simulation, and about what kind of data actually transfers. That's not glamorous work, but it's where a lot of the real progress is coming from.

Fourth is taste. There are a thousand directions you could go, and most of them are dead ends. The people leading frontier labs have a sense for what's going to matter in two or three years, not just what's publishable next quarter. They're willing to bet on something unfashionable, and they're willing to abandon something that isn't working even when they've invested a lot in it.

And finally, I'd say openness to the broader field. Some of the most important moments in robotics recently came from people sharing hardware designs, datasets, and models, so the whole community could build on them. A lab that pushes the frontier and then helps everyone else get there too, I think that's the kind of lab that really moves things forward.

So it's not just about having the most GPUs or the most robots. It's about asking hard questions, testing them against reality quickly, and having the judgment to know which questions are worth asking.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because "frontier" gets thrown around pretty loosely in robotics right now.

For me, a frontier lab is defined by one thing: it's the place where the uncertainty actually gets resolved. Not where papers get published, not where demos get made, but where the open questions about what works get answered first, and everyone else learns from that answer. In language models that's fairly legible. You scale, you see the loss curve, you know where you stand. In robotics it's much harder, because we don't yet agree on what the loss curve even is.

So I'd break it into maybe three things.

First, the lab has to be running the experiment that nobody else can afford to run, or that nobody else believes in enough to run. In robotics that usually means data. Whoever is collecting real-world manipulation data at a scale that makes the rest of the field uncomfortable, and is honest about what that data buys them, that's a frontier lab. If your results are all on a benchmark that fits on one desk, you're doing good science, but you're not at the frontier.

Second, the lab has to be learning things that transfer. A lot of robotics work is beautiful but brittle. One robot, one lab, one lighting condition. A frontier lab is producing results where, when you change the embodiment or the task, the lesson survives. The lesson might be "this architecture generalizes," or it might be "this doesn't, and here's why." Both count. Negative results at scale are incredibly valuable right now, and almost nobody shares them.

Third, and this is the part people underrate, the lab has to be unusually good at the boring parts. Hardware reliability, teleoperation pipelines, evaluation protocols that aren't gameable. In LLM world, the infrastructure is mostly solved and shared. In robotics, every lab rebuilds it, badly, and that's where most of the time goes. The labs that have made the boring parts a solved problem internally are the ones that can actually iterate on the interesting questions.

What I'd push back on is the idea that frontier means the biggest model or the flashiest humanoid. There are groups with enormous compute and impressive videos that, if you look closely, haven't told the field anything it didn't already suspect. And there are smaller groups that ran one careful study and shifted how everyone thinks about, say, how much data you need per task. The second group is more "frontier" to me, even if their press is quieter.

The honest answer is that robotics may not have a frontier lab yet in the sense that language modeling does. We have several candidates, and we have a lot of money, but we don't yet have the thing where one lab's result forces everyone else to update. When that happens, I think we'll all know it.

astra-6.text:
I think a frontier robotics lab needs to do more than get a robot to perform an impressive task once. It needs to push on a limitation that matters, and then show that the progress holds up beyond the conditions of the demo.

For example, can the robot handle an unfamiliar object or a change in its environment? When it makes a mistake, can it recover? And how much human engineering does it take to get it working in a new setting? Those questions help distinguish a more general capability from a carefully constructed demonstration.

I’d also look at how the lab learns from experiments. Robotics brings together learning, hardware, control, and interaction with the physical world. A strong lab can connect those pieces and use failures to decide what to investigate next.

So for me, being a frontier lab is about opening up possibilities that other people can build on, with evidence that makes clear both what works and where the limits still are.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a frontier robotics lab has to do more than make a robot perform an impressive task. It has to push on a limitation that matters, and show that its approach works beyond the particular setup it was built for.

In robotics, that’s a demanding standard because the physical world exposes your assumptions very quickly. A system might work in one room, with one object, under one lighting condition. The interesting question is: what happens when those things change? How much new data, engineering, or human intervention does it need?

So I would look at the questions the lab chooses, how quickly it can test ideas on real hardware, and how honestly it measures progress. Does it understand why something worked? Can it learn from failures? Are its results giving the field a capability or an insight that other people can build on?

For me, being at the frontier is less about having the most polished demonstration and more about consistently turning important unknowns into knowledge.
